# Anatomy of a Model Server: What Happens Per Request

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against PyTorch 2.14 CUDA notes and `torch.compile` docs, the nvidia-smi documentation, NVIDIA TensorRT docs (dynamic shapes, `latest`), the Python glossary (GIL), the py-spy README, and the M/M/1 queue formula. The Python snippet was run locally.

Scope: general model-serving concepts, in the style of Triton, TorchServe and ONNX Runtime servers (open-source programs that load a model and answer requests for it) and hand-rolled FastAPI or gRPC wrappers (your own thin web or RPC layer around a model). This lesson says nothing about how any particular company's serving stack is built. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

Builds on: how a GPU runs work (lesson gpu-fundamentals/01-gpu-architecture-and-roofline); processes, threads and the GIL are explained in this lesson.

## The problem and why it matters

A model server (a program that holds a trained model, meaning a file of learned numbers called weights plus the math that applies them, and answers requests with its predictions) turns "bytes in" into "predictions out" while keeping an expensive device (usually a GPU, a chip built to do the same arithmetic on thousands of numbers at once) busy. Most production pain is not "the model is wrong". It is "latency is fine on average but users complain", "the first request after a deploy is slow", or "adding replicas (more identical copies of the server) did not help".

To operate one you need a model in your head: what work happens per request, where requests wait, and what limits concurrency. With that, "why is p99 bad?" (p99 is the latency that 99 of every 100 requests beat, so it describes the slowest tail) becomes a split of one number into four.

## First principles

1. **A model server is a queue in front of a scarce resource.** The GPU runs kernels (small programs launched onto the GPU; unrelated to the OS kernel) from a queue. Requests that arrive while it is busy wait. Most latency problems are waiting problems, not computing problems.
2. **Latency and throughput are different goals.** Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many finish per second. Batching (running several requests through the model together) raises throughput and usually raises latency. You choose per workload.
3. **Cold is not warm.** The first request pays for things later ones do not: loading weights, creating the CUDA context (per-process state that NVIDIA's CUDA software sets up before a process can use the GPU), choosing kernels, compiling, filling caches. Measure warm and cold separately.
4. **GPU calls are asynchronous.** PyTorch's docs (PyTorch is the Python library most models are written in) say GPU operations are asynchronous by default: Python returns before the work finishes, and errors can show up later at a different line. Timing without synchronising (explicitly waiting for the GPU to finish) measures nothing useful.
5. **Concurrency has three levels.** Processes, threads inside a process, and model instances on a device. A process is a running program with its own memory; threads are separate lines of execution sharing one process's memory. Each has a different cost and a different failure mode.
6. **Averages hide tails.** Latency is queue wait plus service time. As utilisation (the fraction of time the resource is busy) approaches 100%, queue wait grows much faster than load does. The slowest few percent of requests are where users and SLOs (service-level objectives: latency targets you promise, such as "p99 under 200 ms") live.

## How it works

### One request, five stages

```
 client
   │  request (bytes)
   ▼
┌──────────────┐  CPU
│ 1 decode &   │  parse, resize, tokenise
│   preprocess │
└──────┬───────┘
       ▼
┌──────────────┐  CPU, waiting
│ 2 queue &    │  wait for peers or a
│   batch      │  free model instance
└──────┬───────┘
       ▼
┌──────────────┐  CPU -> GPU -> CPU
│ 3 forward    │  copy in, run kernels,
│   pass       │  copy out
└──────┬───────┘
       ▼
┌──────────────┐  CPU
│ 4 postprocess│  argmax, decode, format
└──────┬───────┘
       ▼
   response
```

In the diagram, tokenising means splitting text into the integer pieces a model reads, the forward pass is one run of the input through the model, and argmax picks the highest-scoring output.

Stage 0, before any request, is **load**: read weights from disk, move them to the GPU, build or select the runtime graph (the model's computation written out as a graph of operations). A server that is "up" but has not finished stage 0 is not ready.

Per-request latency is the sum of those stages plus network. When someone says "the model is slow", ask which box. Preprocessing in Python is often the slowest box and it runs on the CPU.

### Where the waiting is

```
 arrivals ──▶ [ request queue ] ──▶ batcher
                                      │
                      ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
                      ▼               ▼               ▼
                 instance A      instance B      instance C
                      │               │               │
                      └───────┬───────┴───────┬───────┘
                              ▼               ▼
                       ┌────────────────────────┐
                       │  GPU: kernel queue     │
                       │  (one device, runs     │
                       │   work in stream order)│
                       └────────────────────────┘
```

Instances are copies of the model, or execution contexts, that let several batches be in flight at once. They all feed one device, whose kernel queue is the list of GPU work waiting to run. If the device is the bottleneck, more instances only move the waiting from the request queue into the GPU queue, and your metrics get harder to read.

### Three levels of concurrency

The table mentions the GIL: CPython's global interpreter lock, which lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. It is always released during I/O and by some native extensions, and Python 3.13 added a build option that disables it; the rest of this lesson assumes the default build.

```
 level        what it is          main cost / risk
 ─────        ──────────          ────────────────
 process      own Python, own     memory per copy,
              CUDA context        GPU memory per ctx
 thread       shared process      GIL for Python
                                  code, races
 instance     model copy or       GPU memory per
              exec context        copy, GPU contention
```

Rule of thumb: Python threads help when time is spent in I/O (waiting on disk or network) or in native code that releases the GIL; they do not speed up Python preprocessing. More processes help CPU-bound preprocessing but each holds its own CUDA context and weights unless you share them. Check what your server does by default before you tune.

### Why p99 is not the average

Take 100 requests, 98 fast and 2 very slow (hypothetical, for illustration):

```python
lat = [20] * 98 + [400, 450]           # ms, hypothetical
lat.sort()
mean = sum(lat) / len(lat)
p99 = lat[-2]                          # nearest-rank p99 of 100 samples
print(mean, p99)                       # mean 28.1, p99 400.0
```

The mean moves by a few milliseconds while the p99 is twenty times the typical request. This script was run locally and printed `28.1 400`. Averages also cannot be combined across servers: you must merge histograms (counts of requests per latency range) or keep the raw samples.

Queueing makes tails worse. In the simplest single-server model (M/M/1: random arrivals, random service, one server), mean time in system is 1/(service rate minus arrival rate). Hypothetical: service rate 50 requests/s means 20 ms each. At 25 requests/s arrival, mean time is 1/25 s = 40 ms. At 45 requests/s it is 1/5 s = 200 ms. The server is 90% busy and requests take ten times their service time. Real servers are not M/M/1, but the shape is true: **the last 10% of utilisation is expensive**.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** after a deploy, mean latency is unchanged but p99 doubled. GPU utilisation shows about 60%, so "the GPU is not the bottleneck".

1. **Split the number.** Do you export per-stage timings (preprocess, queue, forward, postprocess)? If not, add them first. A single end-to-end latency cannot be debugged.
2. **Is the extra time in the queue?** Queue time up with GPU not saturated suggests the batcher's wait or too few instances, not slow compute.
3. **Is the extra time in the forward pass?** Look for spikes tied to new input shapes (the array dimensions of the input; a tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers). Some runtimes compile or tune per shape, and a new shape means a one-off stall. PyTorch's `torch.compile` (which compiles a model into faster code) can recompile when it sees new shapes, and a TensorRT engine (NVIDIA's compiled, GPU-specific form of a model; lesson 03) is tuned for the shape range in its optimisation profile. NVIDIA's dynamic-shapes page does not say what happens outside that range, so test your real shapes.
4. **Is it periodic?** Spikes every N seconds suggest garbage collection (the runtime's automatic memory cleanup, which can pause code), a metrics flush, a cache eviction or a logging thread. A profiler (a tool that samples where a program spends its time) or `py-spy` (one for running Python processes) will show it.
5. **Is it CPU contention?** Preprocessing threads fighting the request threads for cores raises tails without touching the GPU. Check CPU run-queue length (how many threads wait for a free core) and per-core use.
6. **Is it only some replicas?** Compare p99 per replica. One slow node (thermal throttling: the chip slowing itself when hot; a noisy neighbour: another workload sharing the machine; a different GPU driver) drags the global p99.
7. **Is "60% GPU utilisation" what you think?** nvidia-smi (NVIDIA's command-line tool for GPU status) documents GPU utilisation as the percent of time over the past sample period during which one or more kernels were executing (the sample period is between 1 second and 1/6 second, depending on the product). It says nothing about how many cores were busy or whether the GPU was waiting on your CPU.

**Fix:** depends on the branch. A shape stall: pad or bucket (add filler, or group inputs by size; lesson 02) to known shapes and warm them at startup. Contention: pin preprocessing to its own pool or move it off the request path. A bad node: drain it (stop sending it requests). Do not simply add replicas before you know which stage grew.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| One process per GPU: simple, one CUDA context, easy to reason about | Preprocessing is CPU-heavy and starves the GPU |
| Several instances per GPU: overlaps one batch's CPU work with another's GPU work | GPU memory is tight; each instance may cost weights plus workspace (scratch GPU memory used while computing) |
| Several processes: isolates crashes and the GIL | Weights are huge and cannot be duplicated per process |
| Optimise for p99: set queue limits and timeouts | Offline bulk scoring, where throughput is all that matters |

## Interview questions

1. Walk me through what a model server does for one request. *Probe:* where does the first request differ from the hundredth? *Outline:* decode, preprocess, queue/batch, forward pass, postprocess; load and warmup happen before traffic; cold start pays for context, weights, kernel selection or compilation.
2. Why can p99 get worse while the mean stays flat? *Probe:* how would you prove it? *Outline:* mean hides a small slow fraction; split latency by stage; histograms not averages; queueing grows sharply near saturation.
3. What is the difference between latency and throughput, and how does batching move them? *Outline:* batching amortises fixed costs across items (throughput up) but each item waits for peers and for a bigger kernel (latency up).
4. Why are GPU timings from `time.time()` around a PyTorch call wrong? *Outline:* launches are asynchronous; synchronise first, or use CUDA events (timestamps recorded on the GPU's own timeline).
5. Process, thread, instance: when do you add each? *Outline:* the three-level table above, with GPU memory as the limit.
6. The GPU shows 60% utilisation but requests queue. What do you check? *Outline:* the metric means "a kernel was running", not "full"; look at batch size, CPU stalls, instance count.

**Worked exercise:** draw the five-stage pipeline for an image classifier. Mark which stage runs on CPU and which on GPU, then say which three timings you would export first and why.

## Checklist

1. I can list the stages of one request and say where each runs.
2. I can explain cold start versus warm and what is paid once.
3. I can say why GPU timing needs synchronisation.
4. I can explain process versus thread versus instance and the cost of each.
5. I can explain why p99 needs per-stage timings and histograms to debug.

## Common wrong answers

- "Add more replicas." Only if you know the bottleneck is capacity and not one stage or one bad node.
- "GPU utilisation is low so the GPU is fine." The metric is coarse; low utilisation often means the CPU side is starving it.
- "Use threads for parallelism." Python threads do not parallelise Python code under the GIL.
- "Average latency is the SLO." Tails are what users feel.

## Sources

Consulted and checked:
- PyTorch CUDA semantics (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/cuda.html): "By default, GPU operations are asynchronous", errors reported only after the operation executes, `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`, timing with `torch.cuda.synchronize()` or CUDA events.
- nvidia-smi documentation (https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/nvidia-smi/index.html): GPU utilisation definition and sample period; thermal slowdown throttle reasons.
- torch.compile docs (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.compile.html): `dynamic=None` detects dynamism and compiles a more dynamic kernel on recompile.
- TensorRT dynamic shapes (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/dynamic-shapes-basics.html): profile min, opt, max feed the auto-tuner. The page does not say what happens outside the range.
- CUDA programming guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/03-advanced/driver-api.html): "A CUDA context is analogous to a CPU process."
- Python glossary, GIL entry (https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock): one thread runs bytecode at a time, GIL released during I/O and by some extensions, optional free-threaded build from 3.13.
- py-spy README (https://github.com/benfred/py-spy): a sampling profiler that attaches without restarting the program.
- M/M/1 queue (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M/M/1_queue): mean time in system 1/(mu - lambda). Arithmetic in the lesson re-checked by hand; the p99 snippet was run locally.

Not checked against a primary source: how a given server's default instance or thread settings behave, and the generic suggestions in the worked scenario (garbage-collection pauses, metrics flushes, noisy neighbours), which are candidate causes to test, not claims about any tool.
